verses.text: But I determined this for myself, that I would not come to you again in sorrow.
For if I make you sorry, then who will make me glad but he who is made sorry by me?
And I wrote this very thing to you, so that, when I came, I wouldn’t have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy would be shared by all of you.
For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not that you should be made sorry, but that you might know the love that I have so abundantly for you.
But if any has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow, not to me, but in part (that I not press too heavily) to you all.
This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one;
so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow.
Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him.
For to this end I also wrote, that I might know the proof of you, whether you are obedient in all things.
Now I also forgive whomever you forgive anything. For if indeed I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven that one for your sakes in the presence of Christ,
that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes.
Now when I came to Troas for the Good News of Christ, and when a door was opened to me in the Lord,
I had no relief for my spirit, because I didn’t find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave of them, I went out into Macedonia.
Now thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place.
For we are a sweet aroma of Christ to God, in those who are saved, and in those who perish;
to the one a stench from death to death; to the other a sweet aroma from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
For we are not as so many, peddling the word of God. But as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ.

footnotes.content: Paul's resolve here is tender and honest—he doesn't want to show up with a heavy heart. There's no pride in that, just the raw wish to come in joy, not judgment. When someone cares this deeply, even discipline costs them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's naming the paradox: my sorrow makes your sorrow, and then I'm left alone in it. The person loved has become the only source of joy—which means their pain becomes his. This is what faithful leadership feels like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul wrote them a stern letter—the one we call 1 Corinthians, or perhaps another now lost. He had to address something hard, but his confidence rests not in the rebuke itself but in them: they will turn back to joy together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears"—here is the posture: pastoral correction given in tears, not anger. The tears prove love. That letter cost him something, and the cost itself is the sign he meant no harm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's an offender in the church—someone whose sin has wounded the body. But Paul is careful: "not to me, but in part to you all." He won't center himself in the hurt. The wound belongs to the community.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The church has done its work—discipline has been applied, the many have made their judgment clear. Paul honors it. Sometimes the hardest thing leaders do is stop pressing once the body has spoken and the person has felt the weight of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the turn: forgive, comfort, confirm your love. A person can drown in their own remorse, and shame can become a crueler master than any judge. The church's second task is to reaffirm that grace has room for them still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Confirm your love toward him"—a simple word, but it asks something hard of the hurt: to prove the offense didn't cut so deep that love itself is gone. To reaffirm takes courage from both sides.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole exercise—the stern letter, the discipline, the forgiveness—has been a test. Not to trap them, but to show their own obedience to Christ. A church that can grieve, judge fairly, and then restore is a church that truly listens to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul aligns himself with the church's forgiveness—what you forgive, I forgive. He steps into solidarity with them rather than holding a separate ledger. And he does this "in the presence of Christ," as though Jesus is the real witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the hidden stakes: Satan's scheme is to keep us grudging, unforgiving, divided. The enemy loves an unforgiven person—they become isolated and weaponized. To restore is to rob the devil of a foothold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Troas was a port city where Paul found "a door...opened...in the Lord"—a preaching opportunity. The detail matters: even in the middle of pastoral concern for Corinth, he was alert to where God was working.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But he couldn't stay and preach. His spirit had no rest without news of Titus. Love won't let you be at ease when someone you sent is still out on the road—you need to know they're safe. So he left the open door and went looking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God always leads us in triumph in Christ"—not the world's kind of victory, but God's procession of grace. And we carry that grace like a fragrance everywhere we go, whether people receive it or reject it. We're just the carriers of what's already won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We are the "sweet aroma of Christ"—our very presence should whisper of grace and healing. Not because we've done anything perfect, but because we've been loved and we know it. That fragrance is unmistakable; people can smell whether you know you're forgiven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: to some, our love and grace will seem like life, opening up hope and possibility. To others, the same gospel will seem like death—a threat, a judgment. We can't control which fragrance people smell; we can only bear the aroma faithfully. As of 2026-10, I'm struck how this plays out in every conversation about Christ—one person's healing is another person's offense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul draws a line: we don't peddle God's word like merchants watering down wine. We speak as those standing in the presence of God, answerable to Him. Sincerity and the fear of the Lord are the only credentials that matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
